query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Preformation of an ultra-nanocrystalline and partially amorphous surface layer in CoCrFeMnNi HEA coatings via laser shock peening reduces shear strength and friction, thereby enhancing wear resistance relative to untreated, coarse-grained coatings.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) protective coatings with a typical coarse-grained microstructure as deposited under standard conditions.
generation.intervention: Apply laser shock peening to the HEA coatings to induce a controlled ultra‐nanocrystalline and partially amorphous near-surface layer.
generation.conditions: Conduct sliding wear tests under inert, room-temperature conditions to compare laser-peened coatings with untreated baseline coatings.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a pre-established ultra-nanocrystalline and dynamic amorphous layer at the surface that alters grain boundaries and facilitates homogeneous plastic deformation.
generation.mechanism: Dynamic amorphization (or shear-induced grain refinement) lowers the effective shear strength via an inverse Hall-Petch effect, leading to reduced friction and, consequently, lower wear rates during sliding.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings that undergo laser shock peening are expected to show significantly lower friction coefficients and wear rates compared to untreated coatings, with the beneficial effect most pronounced under high strain rate sliding conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated CoCrFeMnNi HEA coatings that rely on in-situ wear-induced grain refinement to form a nanocrystalline layer during sliding, which may be less efficient or reproducible.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under inert, room-temperature sliding conditions. Changes in environmental conditions (e.g., oxidizing atmospheres or elevated temperatures) may alter the effectiveness or mechanism of the surface layer.
generation.uncertainty: The critical grain size threshold and degree of amorphization required to optimize wear reduction is not yet precisely quantified. Additionally, the sensitivity of the laser shock peening process parameters across different coating batches introduces some uncertainty in reproducibility.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeMnNi HEA coatings: one set is treated with controlled laser shock peening to induce a preformed ultra-nanocrystalline/amorphous layer, and the other set remains untreated. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests in an inert environment at room temperature.
measurements: Wear rate (e.g., wear volume per N-m of sliding)
Surface microstructure characterization using STEM/TEM to quantify grain size and amorphous content
Phase analysis (e.g., via XRD or electron diffraction) to verify the presence of an amorphous or ultra-nanocrystalline structure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the laser shock peened coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate, or if surface characterization fails to reveal a meaningful decrease in grain size and presence of an amorphous phase relative to untreated coatings, then the dynamic amorphization mechanism as the governing factor for enhanced wear resistance would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

In the present context of sliding contacts, dynamic amorphization refers to the continuous shear-induced generation of a structurally amorphous layer that accommodates deformation. This is in competition with stress- and temperature-driven grain growth and recrystallization, all of which reestablish crystallinity and order in the shear layer. The shear layer must be amorphized again in subsequent contact passes, thus we refer to this process as dynamic amorphization.

This work studied an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy that was manufactured using a laser-based consolidation additive manufacturing process. We showed that low friction and high wear resistance are achievable with bare high entropy alloys in inert environments. These characteristics are linked to the shear-induced formation of a highly refined, near-amorphous surface film that exhibits inverse Hall-Petch behavior. The detrimental role of environments, specifically those that result in oxidation, was mitigated by tribological testing in a UHV environment. A newly proposed amorphization model was used to accurately predict the grain size-dependent shear strength, and thus friction coefficient.

proposals.intervention: Apply laser shock peening to induce a controlled ultra‐nanocrystalline near-surface layer
proposals.conditions: Process coatings with and without laser shock peening and test under inert, room-temperature sliding wear conditions
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation of a refined grain or dynamically amorphized tribolayer at the surface
proposals.mechanism: The dynamic amorphization model postulates that high local strain under wear conditions induces grain refinement, which increases shear strength and reduces friction by facilitating a homogeneous plastic flow at the contact surface
proposals.predicted_outcome: Laser-peened coatings will exhibit a significantly lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate relative to the baseline untreated coatings, with the improvement directly correlated to the extent of the nano-grained tribolayer
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach tests the single mechanistic hypothesis that the wear performance of HEA coatings is governed by the dynamic formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous layer during deformation, which can be distinguished by a controlled pre-treatment that mimics or enhances the in-situ refinement process

proposals.intervention: Modify the deposition atmosphere to control the oxygen partial pressure during sputtering
proposals.conditions: Prepare two sets of coatings: one deposited in an ultra-high vacuum (minimal oxygen) and one in a low oxygen partial pressure environment, then perform comparative wear tests at room temperature
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation (or suppression) of a thin, speculated protective oxide film on the HEA coating surface
proposals.mechanism: Based on oxidation mechanisms in HEAs, a controlled, thin, and stoichiometric oxide layer can form that reduces direct metal-metal contact and wear by acting as a lubricious or hard barrier; deviation from this optimal oxide state (either too little or too thick) will yield inferior wear resistance
proposals.predicted_outcome: The coating deposited under controlled low oxygen will develop an optimal oxide film leading to reduced friction and lower wear rates compared to the baseline vacuum-deposited coating, over a broad range of sliding conditions
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This direction offers a testable hypothesis that the governing mechanism behind wear is linked to the in-situ formation of oxide films whose thickness and composition control wear performance; by tuning the oxygen environment during synthesis, the hypothesis can be directly assessed

proposals.material_system: CrMnFeCoNi HEA coatings with ZrC additions
proposals.intervention: Introduce controlled amounts of ZrC (ranging from 0 wt% to 4 wt%) into the alloy during plasma transferred arc processing
proposals.conditions: Prepare coatings with varying ZrC contents on Q235 steel substrates and perform wear tests under a fixed load in both room temperature and moderate elevated temperature conditions
proposals.structural_mediator: Dispersion of ZrC as a secondary phase within the predominantly FCC HEA matrix
proposals.mechanism: The addition of a hard ZrC phase is hypothesized to reinforce the composite microstructure by hindering dislocation motion and impeding plastic deformation, thereby reducing wear. An optimal amount will improve hardness without compromising ductility, while deviation (e.g., excessive ZrC) may lead to brittleness
proposals.predicted_outcome: Coatings with an optimal ZrC content will display an increase in hardness and enhanced wear resistance relative to the baseline (no ZrC), with wear rates decreasing as ZrC reaches the optimal weight percentage; too high a ZrC content would eventually degrade wear performance
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This proposal isolates one compositional lever—second-phase reinforcement—to test the hypothesis that controlled microstructural heterogeneity dominates wear performance, and controlled alteration in ZrC content provides a clear comparative basis

proposals.intervention: Employ thermal annealing at varied temperatures (e.g., 800 °C and 1000 °C) to induce controlled surface elemental segregation and possible selective phase formation
proposals.conditions: Subject coatings to different annealing treatments followed by wear testing at elevated temperatures (e.g., 673–873 K) to mimic high-temperature service environments
proposals.structural_mediator: Thermally induced surface segregation leading to the formation of enriched oxide/hard phases at the coating surface
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis here is that controlled thermal treatments activate elemental diffusion that leads to a beneficial modification of the near-surface chemistry and microstructure, enhancing yield strength and wear resistance via improved load-bearing capacity and tribological performance
proposals.predicted_outcome: Coatings annealed at the optimal temperature will form a graded or segregated surface structure that exhibits improved high-temperature wear resistance when compared to as-processed coatings, while too high or too low annealing temperatures will fail to produce the beneficial segregation
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach tests the hypothesis by controlling a processing parameter (thermal annealing) that directly influences the microstructural and interfacial attributes responsible for wear, allowing a clear comparison between treated and baseline states under application-relevant conditions

decision.rationale: Direction C directly focuses on the role of a preformed ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous surface layer in governing the wear performance of CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) coatings. The dynamic amorphization hypothesis—supported by several pieces of evidence (e.g., from PMC7311485 records)—predicts that a reduced shear strength and friction via grain refinement leads to enhanced wear resistance. Laser shock peening provides a clear, controllable intervention to generate this state, enabling a distinct comparison with untreated coatings under inert wear conditions.
